definition: No longer used because something newer and better has replaced it.
examples: My old phone is obsolete; the apps no longer work on it.
Many office skills become obsolete when new software arrives.

pattern.example: Fax machines have become obsolete.

cloze.sentence: Floppy disks are ___ now; nobody sells computers with a drive for them.

formDrill.sentence: Critics call it planned ___: products are made to stop working after a few years.

fix.wrong: This machine is obsolete from the new model.
fix.right: This machine has been made obsolete by the new model.
fix.why: Use "made obsolete by" to show what replaced it.

distractors: Still in fashion and used by most people.
Easy to repair when it breaks.
Too expensive for ordinary people to buy.
tip: Obsolete is stronger than "old": an old thing may still work, an obsolete thing is no longer useful.

definition: The best possible for a particular situation; giving the best result.
examples: Sleeping seven to eight hours is optimal for most adults.
We chose the optimal route to avoid the Lagos traffic.

pattern.example: The temperature is optimal for growing tomatoes.

cloze.sentence: The app works at its ___ speed only when you have a strong internet signal.

formDrill.sentence: She arranged the shelves to use the space ___.

fix.wrong: This is the most optimal solution.
fix.right: This is the optimal solution.
fix.why: Optimal already means "best", so do not add "most" or "more".

distractors: Good enough but not very impressive.
The cheapest choice available.
Chosen by most people in a group.
tip: Do not say "more optimal" or "most optimal"; use "optimal" alone.

definition: To trust someone or something to do what you need, or to depend on them.
examples: Many families rely on money sent from relatives abroad.
You can rely on Tunde to finish the work on time.

pattern.example: She relies on public transport to get to work.

cloze.sentence: I do not have a car, so I ___ on my brother for lifts.

formDrill.sentence: A ___ internet connection is vital for remote work.

fix.wrong: You can rely in me.
fix.right: You can rely on me.
fix.why: "Rely" always takes the preposition "on" (or "upon").

distractors: To search carefully for a missing item.
To refuse help from other people.
To repeat something many times to remember it.
tip: Rely is followed by "on", never "in" or "to". The noun is "reliance", not "relyance".

definition: Continuing to try or to exist for a long time, even when it is difficult or annoying.
examples: Her persistent effort finally got her the scholarship.
I have a persistent cough that will not go away.

pattern.example: He is persistent in chasing late payments.

cloze.sentence: The company has a ___ problem with late deliveries that nobody has fixed.

formDrill.sentence: Her ___ finally earned her the promotion.

fix.wrong: She is very persistent to learn French.
fix.right: She is very persistent in learning French.
fix.why: Use "persistent in" + -ing for the thing you keep doing.

distractors: Easily distracted by small things.
Ready to give up at the first problem.
Happening only once in a while.
tip: Persistent can be positive (a determined person) or negative (a persistent problem or an annoying salesperson).

definition: Exact and accurate in every detail, with no mistakes.
examples: Please give me the precise time of the meeting.
The doctor was precise about how much medicine to take.

pattern.example: Be more precise about the budget.

cloze.sentence: The recipe needs ___ measurements, or the cake will not rise.

formDrill.sentence: He described the problem very ___, so we fixed it quickly.

fix.wrong: Can you be more precise in the date?
fix.right: Can you be more precise about the date?
fix.why: Use "precise about" for the topic you want exact details on.

distractors: Rough and based on a guess.
Friendly but a little too talkative.
Short enough to read very quickly.
tip: "Precise" is about exact detail; "concise" is about using few words.

definition: Very well known or important; also easy to see.
examples: She is a prominent lawyer who often speaks on the radio.
Put the price in a prominent place so customers can see it.

pattern.rule: prominent + noun / play a prominent role in
pattern.example: He played a prominent role in the project.

cloze.sentence: A ___ businessman donated money to rebuild the school.

formDrill.sentence: The sign was ___ displayed at the entrance.

fix.wrong: He is a prominant lawyer in Lagos.
fix.right: He is a prominent lawyer in Lagos.
fix.why: Spell it prominent, with 'e' after the 'n'.

distractors: Very shy and avoiding attention.
Recently arrived from another place.
Easily upset by criticism.

definition: To change or influence someone or something, often in a negative way.
examples: The fuel price increase will affect everyone who travels by bus.
Stress affected his sleep for months.

pattern.example: Rain can affect our travel plans.

cloze.sentence: The new tax will ___ small businesses the most.

formDrill.sentence: Stress ___ different people in different ways.

fix.wrong: The delay affected on our plans.
fix.right: The delay affected our plans.
fix.why: "Affect" is a transitive verb and takes no preposition.

distractors: To pretend to have a feeling or quality.
To make something bigger or longer.
To end something completely.
tip: Affect is usually a verb ("it affects me"); effect is usually a noun ("it has an effect on me").

definition: Careful and sensible, especially about money or risks, so as to avoid problems later.
examples: It is prudent to save some money before you quit your job.
The bank took a prudent approach and checked every document twice.

pattern.example: It is prudent to back up your files.

cloze.sentence: Keeping three months of salary aside is a ___ choice.

formDrill.sentence: She spends ___ and always compares prices before buying.

fix.wrong: She is prudent of her money.
fix.right: She is prudent with her money.
fix.why: Use 'prudent with' for something you handle carefully.

distractors: Willing to take big risks quickly.
Generous with gifts and favors.
Likely to complain about small things.
tip: Prudent is positive and formal; "careful" is the everyday word.

definition: Not needed because it repeats something else; also, no longer needed in a job.
examples: The phrase "free gift" is redundant because gifts are already free.
Thirty workers were made redundant when the factory closed.

pattern.example: He was made redundant last month.

cloze.sentence: After the merger, two departments became ___ and were closed.

formDrill.sentence: The company announced ten ___ after its sales dropped.

fix.wrong: The company redundant fifty workers.
fix.right: The company made fifty workers redundant.
fix.why: "Redundant" is an adjective; use "made redundant", not a verb.

distractors: Very new and not yet tested.
Quick to respond to messages.
Paid more than other workers.
tip: In British and Nigerian English, "made redundant" means losing your job because it is no longer needed, not because of poor work.

definition: Very strict, thorough and careful, leaving nothing to chance.
examples: The medicine went through rigorous testing before it was approved.
Our teacher has rigorous standards for homework.

pattern.example: The school has a rigorous selection process.

cloze.sentence: Soldiers go through ___ training before they are sent out.

formDrill.sentence: The data was ___ checked by two analysts.

fix.wrong: The test was very rigorously.
fix.right: The test was very rigorous.
fix.why: "Rigorous" is an adjective; use "rigorously" only to describe a verb.

distractors: Calm and relaxed about rules.
Easy to finish in very little time.
Created in a sudden, spontaneous way.

definition: A change that is caused by something; a result.
examples: The new law had a big effect on small shops.
Social media can have a harmful effect on teenagers.

pattern.example: The strike had a bad effect on prices.

cloze.sentence: The medicine has no ___ on my headache.

formDrill.sentence: The new rule is ___ at making people arrive on time.

fix.wrong: The rain had a big affect on the match.
fix.right: The rain had a big effect on the match.
fix.why: "Effect" is the noun; "affect" is the verb.

distractors: A reason that makes something happen.
A feeling of being very tired.
A plan made before an event.
tip: Remember: "affect" is the action (verb), "effect" is the result (noun). Cause leads to effect.

definition: Strong and able to work well even in difficult conditions.
examples: The company has a robust plan to survive the economic crisis.
These phones are robust enough to survive a fall.

pattern.example: They built a robust payment system.

cloze.sentence: The country has a ___ economy that grew every year.

formDrill.sentence: The software must be tested for ___ before launch.

fix.wrong: This phone is robustness enough to survive a fall.
fix.right: This phone is robust enough to survive a fall.
fix.why: Use the adjective 'robust' before 'enough', not the noun.

distractors: Soft and easily damaged.
Very fast and light.
Cheap and quickly made.

definition: Doubtful about whether something is true or will work; not easily convinced.
examples: I am skeptical about any offer that promises quick money.
Her boss was skeptical of the new plan.

pattern.example: She is skeptical about online investment schemes.

cloze.sentence: Be ___ when a stranger asks for your bank details.

formDrill.sentence: His ___ made him check every claim before believing it.

fix.wrong: I am skeptical to his story.
fix.right: I am skeptical about his story.
fix.why: Use "skeptical about" or "skeptical of".

distractors: Very excited and full of hope.
Unable to make a decision.
Interested in learning new things.
tip: British spelling is sceptical; both are correct. It means doubtful, not rude or negative.

definition: Complex and advanced in design; also having good taste and wide experience of life.
examples: Banks use sophisticated software to detect fraud.
She is a sophisticated woman who has traveled to many countries.

pattern.example: They installed a sophisticated alarm system.

cloze.sentence: The thieves used a ___ method to avoid the cameras.

formDrill.sentence: The restaurant has a modern look and real ___.

fix.wrong: The system is very sophisticate.
fix.right: The system is very sophisticated.
fix.why: The adjective ends in "-ed": "sophisticated".

distractors: Simple and easy for anyone to use.
Very old and no longer fashionable.
Rude and lacking good manners.
tip: It does not mean "fake"; the older meaning of "spoiled" is no longer used.

definition: To say that you are unhappy or not satisfied with something.
examples: Customers complained about the long queue at the bank.
Stop complaining and help me carry these boxes.

pattern.rule: complain + about + noun; complain to + person
pattern.example: She complained to the manager about the noise.

cloze.sentence: If the food is cold, you should ___ to the waiter.

formDrill.sentence: He wrote a formal ___ to the airline after losing his bag.

fix.wrong: They complained the service.
fix.right: They complained about the service.
fix.why: "Complain" needs "about" before the thing you are unhappy with.

distractors: To praise someone in front of others.
To ask a friend for advice.
To explain a rule to a customer.
tip: Complain about the problem, complain to the person. "Complain of" is used for pain or illness: "She complained of a headache."

definition: Done naturally and suddenly, without planning or being forced.
examples: We took a spontaneous trip to the beach on Saturday.
The crowd gave a spontaneous cheer when she walked in.

pattern.example: It was a spontaneous decision to move abroad.

cloze.sentence: The party was ___; we decided to have it that morning.

formDrill.sentence: People ___ started singing when the power came back.

fix.wrong: He reacted spontaneous to the news.
fix.right: He reacted spontaneously to the news.
fix.why: Use the adverb "spontaneously" to describe a verb.

distractors: Carefully planned many weeks ahead.
Done only because someone ordered it.
Very serious and formal.

definition: Large in amount, size or importance.
examples: She received a substantial bonus at the end of the year.
There is substantial evidence that the road is unsafe.

pattern.example: The project needs a substantial investment.

cloze.sentence: The company made a ___ profit this quarter.

formDrill.sentence: Rent has risen ___ in the past year.

fix.wrong: There was a substantial amounts of rain.
fix.right: There was a substantial amount of rain.
fix.why: "Amount" is singular after "a".

distractors: Very small but important.
Real and made of physical material.
Likely to change very soon.
tip: Substantial is more formal than "big" and is often used for money, evidence and change.

definition: Able to continue for a long time without harming the environment or running out of resources.
examples: Many farmers are switching to sustainable methods that protect the soil.
Working sixteen hours a day is not sustainable.

pattern.example: Solar power is a sustainable source of energy.

cloze.sentence: The company wants to use only ___ materials in its packaging.

formDrill.sentence: The city is planning for long-term ___ of its water supply.

fix.wrong: The farm uses sustainability methods.
fix.right: The farm uses sustainable methods.
fix.why: Use the adjective 'sustainable' before a noun, not the noun.

distractors: Cheap and available everywhere.
Quick to produce in large amounts.
Expensive but of very high quality.

definition: Knowing that something exists or is happening; having knowledge of a situation.
examples: Are you aware that the office will be closed on Friday?
He was not aware of the risks when he signed.

pattern.rule: aware + of + noun / aware + that + clause
pattern.example: I am aware of the problem.

cloze.sentence: Please be ___ that the price may change without notice.

formDrill.sentence: The campaign raises ___ about road safety.

fix.wrong: I was not aware about the meeting.
fix.right: I was not aware of the meeting.
fix.why: "Aware" takes "of", not "about".

distractors: Worried about something that may happen.
Very eager to learn.
Having a strong feeling of being tired.
tip: Aware is usually used with "of"; do not say "aware about".

definition: So long, slow or repetitive that it makes you bored.
examples: Filling in the same form again and again is tedious.
The speech was so tedious that half the room fell asleep.

pattern.rule: tedious + noun / it is tedious + to + verb
pattern.example: It is tedious to count the stock by hand.

cloze.sentence: Entering data into a spreadsheet all day is ___ work.

formDrill.sentence: The ___ of the long journey made the children restless.

fix.wrong: I felt very tedious during the lecture.
fix.right: The lecture was tedious, so I felt bored.
fix.why: 'Tedious' describes the boring thing, not how a person feels.

distractors: Difficult to understand at first.
Exciting and full of surprises.
Done in a hurry and badly.
tip: Tedious is stronger than "boring": it suggests something long and repetitive.

definition: Easy to see through; also open and honest, with nothing hidden.
examples: Glass is transparent, so we can see the garden.
The charity publishes a transparent report on how it spends donations.

pattern.example: The manager was transparent about the changes.

cloze.sentence: The government promised a ___ election process.

formDrill.sentence: Citizens want more ___ in how taxes are spent.

fix.wrong: The company is transparent of its prices.
fix.right: The company is transparent about its prices.
fix.why: Use "transparent about" for what is shared openly.

distractors: Too bright to look at.
Hard to find or reach.
Strong enough to resist damage.

definition: Of very little importance or value.
examples: Do not waste time arguing over trivial matters.
The mistake was trivial, so we ignored it.

pattern.example: It may sound trivial, but the color matters to the client.

cloze.sentence: It is a ___ problem that takes two minutes to fix.

formDrill.sentence: Please do not ___ her complaint; it is serious.

fix.wrong: He treated my problem as a trivia.
fix.right: He treated my problem as trivial.
fix.why: 'Trivia' is a noun for small facts; 'trivial' is the adjective.

distractors: Very urgent and needing quick action.
Difficult to explain to others.
Hidden from most people.

definition: Well known to you because you have seen, heard or experienced it before.
examples: Your face looks familiar; have we met?
I am familiar with this software from my last job.

pattern.rule: familiar + with + noun; familiar + to + person
pattern.example: The route is familiar to me.

cloze.sentence: The name sounds ___, but I cannot remember where I heard it.

formDrill.sentence: New staff need a week to ___ themselves with the system.

fix.wrong: I am not familiar to this city.
fix.right: I am not familiar with this city.
fix.why: Say "I am familiar with X" or "X is familiar to me".

distractors: Related to someone by blood or marriage.
Rude in a friendly way.
Famous all over the world.
tip: Two patterns: "I am familiar with it" and "It is familiar to me".

definition: To weaken something or someone slowly, especially confidence, authority or a plan.
examples: Constant criticism can undermine a child's confidence.
The rumors undermined the manager's authority.

pattern.example: Late payments undermine trust between partners.

cloze.sentence: Cutting corners will ___ the quality of our work.

formDrill.sentence: The report was ___ by several mistakes in the data.

fix.wrong: The scandal undermined to his reputation.
fix.right: The scandal undermined his reputation.
fix.why: "Undermine" is transitive and takes no preposition.

distractors: To explain something in a very simple way.
To delay a decision for a long time.
To protect and support something.

definition: Not clear or exact; lacking detail so that it is hard to understand.
examples: His answer was vague, so I asked again.
I have a vague memory of meeting her at a wedding.

pattern.example: She was vague about her plans.

cloze.sentence: The instructions were so ___ that nobody knew what to do.

formDrill.sentence: I ___ remember the man, but I cannot recall his name.

fix.wrong: She was vague at the details.
fix.right: She was vague about the details.
fix.why: Use 'vague about' a topic.

distractors: Very clear and easy to follow.
Strong and likely to cause anger.
Related to a topic in a direct way.

definition: Easily hurt, attacked or harmed, physically or emotionally.
examples: Small shops are vulnerable to sudden price changes.
Old people living alone can be vulnerable to scams.

pattern.example: Children are vulnerable to infections.

cloze.sentence: The website was ___ to hackers because it had no security.

formDrill.sentence: Sharing your fears shows ___, but it builds trust.

fix.wrong: We are vulnerable for attack.
fix.right: We are vulnerable to attack.
fix.why: "Vulnerable" takes "to".

distractors: Strong enough to defend itself.
Likely to cause harm to others.
Hidden from public view.

definition: Easy to use, or suitable because it saves time or effort.
examples: Mobile banking is convenient because you do not have to visit the branch.
Is Thursday at 3 p.m. convenient for you?

pattern.rule: convenient + for + person; convenient + to + verb
pattern.example: Is this time convenient for you?

cloze.sentence: The flat is ___ for work, only ten minutes from the office.

formDrill.sentence: For your ___, we deliver to your door.

fix.wrong: The time is not convenient to me.
fix.right: The time is not convenient for me.
fix.why: Use "convenient for" + person.

distractors: Cheap and of poor quality.
Very large and hard to move.
Available only to special customers.
tip: You are not "convenient"; a time or place is. Say "Is it convenient for you?"

definition: To be too much for someone to deal with, or to defeat or cover completely.
examples: The number of emails overwhelmed her on Monday morning.
Joy overwhelmed him when he heard the good news.

pattern.rule: overwhelm + person; be overwhelmed by / with + noun
pattern.example: I felt overwhelmed by the amount of work.

cloze.sentence: Too many tasks can ___ new employees in their first week.

formDrill.sentence: She gave an ___ response to the question: no one disagreed.

fix.wrong: I am overwhelming by work.
fix.right: I am overwhelmed by work.
fix.why: Use "overwhelmed" for how you feel, "overwhelming" for what causes it.

distractors: To make someone feel bored and sleepy.
To surprise someone with a gift.
To ask someone for too many favors.
tip: Overwhelmed = the person feels it; overwhelming = the thing that causes it. It can be positive: "overwhelming support".

definition: To keep delaying something you should do, usually because it is boring or difficult.
examples: I always procrastinate when I have to write reports.
He procrastinated for weeks and then paid a late fee.

pattern.example: Stop procrastinating and start your essay.

cloze.sentence: If you ___, the deadline will arrive before you start.

formDrill.sentence: Her ___ cost her the job; she kept delaying every report.

fix.wrong: He procrastinated to call the bank.
fix.right: He procrastinated about calling the bank.
fix.why: Do not use "procrastinate" with a to-infinitive; use "about" + -ing.

distractors: To work very quickly under pressure.
To plan every task in careful detail.
To ask other people to do your work.
tip: Procrastinate is not the same as "forget": you know the task, but you choose to delay it.

definition: Acting early to make things happen instead of waiting for problems to appear.
examples: A proactive manager fixes small issues before they become big ones.
Be proactive: ask for feedback instead of waiting for a review.

pattern.example: She is proactive about asking for new tasks.

cloze.sentence: Our team takes a ___ approach and prevents delays before they happen.

formDrill.sentence: The nurses ___ checked every patient before the storm.

fix.wrong: He is very proactive to solve problems.
fix.right: He is very proactive in solving problems.
fix.why: Use "proactive in" + -ing.

distractors: Reacting only after trouble has happened.
Very active and always busy.
Careful not to spend too much money.
tip: The opposite is "reactive".

definition: Having a certain value, or good enough to deserve your time or effort.
examples: This car is worth about five million naira.
The film is worth watching if you like thrillers.

pattern.example: The book is worth reading twice.

cloze.sentence: Is it ___ paying more for a faster internet plan?

formDrill.sentence: A ___ cause deserves our support.

fix.wrong: It is worth to visit the museum.
fix.right: It is worth visiting the museum.
fix.why: "Worth" is followed by -ing, not a to-infinitive.

distractors: Costing much less than expected.
Very important to a small group of people.
Easy to find in any shop.
tip: Say "worth doing", never "worth to do".

definition: To use something you already have in a way that gives you the most benefit.
examples: She leveraged her network to find a new job.
We can leverage social media to reach more customers.

pattern.example: The company leveraged its brand to launch a new product.

cloze.sentence: Small businesses can ___ free online tools to save money.

formDrill.sentence: By ___ his experience, he negotiated a better salary.

fix.wrong: We leverage on our contacts.
fix.right: We leverage our contacts.
fix.why: "Leverage" is transitive; do not add "on".

distractors: To lift a heavy object using a bar.
To borrow money without paying it back.
To waste a resource through poor planning.
tip: Common in business English; in everyday speech, "use" is often simpler.

definition: Careful and slightly afraid because you think something may be dangerous or dishonest.
examples: Be wary of emails asking for your password.
The farmers were wary of the new loan scheme.

pattern.example: I am wary of sharing my phone number.

cloze.sentence: After being cheated once, he is ___ of strangers who offer deals.

formDrill.sentence: She ___ checked the stairs before stepping onto them.

fix.wrong: I am wary about the strangers.
fix.right: I am wary of strangers.
fix.why: "Wary" normally takes "of".

distractors: Very tired after a long day.
Happy to try something new.
Ready to forgive someone quickly.
tip: Wary is milder than "afraid" and is not the same as "weary" (tired).

definition: Showing a clear and deep understanding of a person or situation.
examples: Her insightful comments helped us see the real problem.
It was an insightful article about why young people change jobs.

pattern.example: He gave an insightful talk about customer habits.

cloze.sentence: The consultant offered an ___ report on why sales fell.

formDrill.sentence: Her ___ into customer needs helped the team improve the app.

fix.wrong: Thank you for your insight comment.
fix.right: Thank you for your insightful comment.
fix.why: The adjective is "insightful"; "insight" is the noun.

distractors: Quick to criticize other people.
Not interested in learning details.
Easy to understand without effort.

definition: To say that something is not true, or to refuse to give or allow something.
examples: He denied taking the money from the till.
The bank denied her request for a loan.

pattern.example: She denied breaking the window.

cloze.sentence: The minister ___ the rumor and called it false.

formDrill.sentence: After the accident, the driver was in ___ and refused to talk.

fix.wrong: He denied to have stolen the phone.
fix.right: He denied stealing the phone.
fix.why: "Deny" is followed by -ing, not a to-infinitive.

distractors: To admit something after a long delay.
To promise to do something soon.
To forget an important fact.
tip: Deny + -ing: "She denied taking it." Do not say "deny to do".

definition: Making you feel nervous or less confident because something seems very difficult.
examples: Moving to a new country alone is a daunting prospect.
The pile of unpaid bills looked daunting.

pattern.rule: daunting + noun / it is daunting + to + verb
pattern.example: It is daunting to speak in front of five hundred people.

cloze.sentence: Starting a business with no savings is a ___ challenge.

formDrill.sentence: Do not let the long list ___ you; take one task at a time.

fix.wrong: I felt very daunting before the exam.
fix.right: I felt daunted before the exam.
fix.why: "Daunting" describes the task; "daunted" describes how you feel.

distractors: Boring and repeating the same steps.
Easy to finish before lunch.
Unfair to some of the people involved.
tip: Daunting describes the task; "daunted" describes the person.

definition: The ability to understand and share another person's feelings.
examples: A good nurse shows empathy for frightened patients.
Managers need empathy to understand why staff are stressed.

pattern.example: She has great empathy for her students.

cloze.sentence: Listening without judging is a sign of ___.

formDrill.sentence: It is hard to ___ with someone whose life is so different from yours.

fix.wrong: He has no empathy to other people.
fix.right: He has no empathy for other people.
fix.why: Use "empathy for" or "empathy with".

distractors: A strong wish to help people for money.
The feeling of being sorry for yourself.
Very strong anger towards someone.
tip: Empathy is feeling WITH someone; sympathy is feeling sorry FOR them.

definition: A difficult situation in which you must choose between two options, neither of which is good.
examples: She faced a dilemma: take the higher salary or stay near her family.
The manager was in a dilemma about whom to promote.

pattern.rule: dilemma + about / over + noun; in a dilemma
pattern.example: He is in a dilemma about which job to accept.

cloze.sentence: I am in a ___: I want to help my friend, but it means missing work.

formDrill.sentence: Doctors often face ethical ___ at work.

fix.wrong: I have a big dilemma to choose a school.
fix.right: I have a big dilemma about choosing a school.
fix.why: Use "dilemma about/over" and not a to-infinitive.

distractors: A small mistake that is easy to correct.
A problem with only one clear answer.
An argument between two close friends.
tip: A dilemma has two hard choices; do not use it for any small problem.

definition: To give someone support or hope so that they do something, or to make something more likely.
examples: Her parents encouraged her to apply for the scholarship.
The new bonus scheme encourages workers to arrive early.

pattern.example: The teacher encouraged us to ask questions.

cloze.sentence: Managers should ___ staff to share their ideas.

formDrill.sentence: Thank you for your constant ___ during my studies.

fix.wrong: He encouraged me applying for the job.
fix.right: He encouraged me to apply for the job.
fix.why: Encourage + person + to + verb, not -ing.

distractors: To order someone to do a task.
To warn someone about a danger.
To make someone feel ashamed.
tip: Encourage someone TO do something; the opposite is "discourage someone FROM doing".

definition: Something that makes people want to do something, such as a reward or a benefit.
examples: The company offers an incentive of free lunch for early arrival.
Lower taxes are an incentive for people to start businesses.

pattern.example: There is little incentive to save when prices rise so fast.

cloze.sentence: The discount is an ___ for customers to pay early.

formDrill.sentence: Companies often ___ staff with extra pay for good results.

fix.wrong: He has no incentive for working harder.
fix.right: He has no incentive to work harder.
fix.why: "Incentive" is followed by "to" + verb.

distractors: A rule that people must obey.
A punishment for breaking a rule.
A report about a problem at work.
tip: Incentive is a reward that encourages action; a "bonus" is one kind of incentive.

definition: Giving all the necessary information in few words.
examples: Please write a concise summary of the meeting.
Her email was short and concise.

pattern.example: Keep your message concise.

cloze.sentence: Managers prefer ___ reports that get to the point quickly.

formDrill.sentence: She explained the rules ___ in two sentences.

fix.wrong: Please be concise on your answer.
fix.right: Please be concise in your answer.
fix.why: Use "in your answer" with "concise".

distractors: Long and full of small details.
Written in a very formal style.
Easy to read aloud to others.
tip: Concise means short but complete; "brief" can mean short but missing detail.

definition: Not very good; of only average or disappointing quality.
examples: The food was mediocre and the service was slow.
He gave a mediocre performance in the interview.

pattern.example: The hotel was mediocre for the price.

cloze.sentence: I expected a great film, but it was ___ at best.

formDrill.sentence: He refused to accept ___ and kept improving his work.

fix.wrong: The food was mediocrity.
fix.right: The food was mediocre.
fix.why: After 'was', use the adjective 'mediocre', not the noun.

distractors: Excellent and better than most.
Very bad and unacceptable.
Expensive and full of detail.
tip: Mediocre is negative: it is worse than "average" because it suggests disappointment.

definition: To think carefully about something before making a decision.
examples: We are considering moving to a bigger flat.
Please consider my offer before you answer.

pattern.example: I am considering changing my job.

cloze.sentence: I will ___ your request and give you an answer tomorrow.

formDrill.sentence: It was very ___ of you to call and check on me.

fix.wrong: I am considering to buy a car.
fix.right: I am considering buying a car.
fix.why: "Consider" is followed by -ing, not a to-infinitive.

distractors: To forget something on purpose.
To ask someone a direct question.
To agree with someone immediately.
tip: Consider + -ing: "I considered leaving". Do not say "consider to leave".

definition: Done without any plan or order, so that the result is careless or random.
examples: The files were stored in a haphazard way, so nothing was easy to find.
Their haphazard planning caused the event to fail.

pattern.rule: haphazard + noun / in a haphazard way
pattern.example: The books were piled in a haphazard way.

cloze.sentence: Boxes were stacked in a ___ way, and one fell on his foot.

formDrill.sentence: The papers were thrown ___ on the desk.

fix.wrong: The room was arranged haphazard.
fix.right: The room was arranged haphazardly.
fix.why: Use the adverb "haphazardly" after a verb.

distractors: Planned in great detail.
Done quickly and neatly.
Done only when someone is watching.

definition: Not certain or final; offered carefully because you are unsure.
examples: We made a tentative plan to meet on Friday.
She gave a tentative smile before speaking.

pattern.example: They reached a tentative agreement on the price.

cloze.sentence: The date for the launch is only ___; it may change.

formDrill.sentence: He ___ suggested a new idea, unsure how the team would react.

fix.wrong: Our plan is still tentatively.
fix.right: Our plan is still tentative.
fix.why: "Tentative" is the adjective; "tentatively" modifies a verb.

distractors: Fixed and impossible to change.
Strongly opposed to something.
Very confident and bold.

definition: Only on the surface; not deep or thorough.
examples: The cut was superficial and healed in a few days.
His knowledge of the subject is superficial.

pattern.example: The report gave only a superficial analysis.

cloze.sentence: A ___ look at the data will not show the real problem.

formDrill.sentence: The two phones are ___ similar, but they work very differently.

fix.wrong: He gave a superficially answer.
fix.right: He gave a superficial answer.
fix.why: Use the adjective "superficial" before a noun.

distractors: Very deep and based on long study.
Related to the top part of a building.
Very friendly and open to others.
tip: It can describe a person who cares only about appearance: "a superficial person".

definition: To make someone agree to do or believe something by giving good reasons.
examples: I persuaded my brother to lend me his laptop.
She was persuaded by the clear evidence in the report.

pattern.rule: persuade + object + to + verb / that + clause
pattern.example: He persuaded her to stay longer.

cloze.sentence: Nothing can ___ me to sign that contract.

formDrill.sentence: She made a ___ argument, and the board agreed.

fix.wrong: I persuaded him for join us.
fix.right: I persuaded him to join us.
fix.why: "Persuade" takes object + to-infinitive.

distractors: To force someone by using threats.
To ask someone a difficult question.
To feel sure about something yourself.

definition: A warm, slightly sad feeling when you think about happy times in the past.
examples: Hearing that old song filled him with nostalgia.
There is a lot of nostalgia for 1990s music.

pattern.example: She felt nostalgia for her school days.

cloze.sentence: Looking at old photos brought back a wave of ___.

formDrill.sentence: He felt ___ when he returned to his childhood home.

fix.wrong: I have nostalgia of my village.
fix.right: I have nostalgia for my village.
fix.why: Use "nostalgia for".

distractors: A strong fear of going outside.
A feeling of anger about the past.
A plan for a future event.
tip: Say "nostalgic for" or "nostalgia for"; you may also feel nostalgic about something.

definition: A friendly relationship in which people understand each other well.
examples: A good teacher builds rapport with students quickly.
There was an easy rapport between the two colleagues.

pattern.example: She has a good rapport with her clients.

cloze.sentence: It takes time to build ___ with a new team.

fix.wrong: He has a good rapport to his boss.
fix.right: He has a good rapport with his boss.
fix.why: Use "rapport with" or "rapport between".

distractors: A written report about a meeting.
A strong argument between two people.
A formal rule about how to behave.
tip: The final "t" is silent: say "ra-POR". Not the same as "report".

definition: To say something again, usually to make a point clear or strong.
examples: I want to reiterate that the deadline will not change.
The manager reiterated his support for the plan.

pattern.example: Let me reiterate our main goal.

cloze.sentence: At the end of the talk, she ___ the key message.

formDrill.sentence: Her ___ of the rules did not change anything.

fix.wrong: I want to reiterate again that we start Monday.
fix.right: I want to reiterate that we start Monday.
fix.why: "Reiterate" already means "say again", so "again" is redundant.

distractors: To change a statement completely.
To ask a question more than once.
To cancel a decision made earlier.
tip: Formal. In everyday speech, say "repeat" or "say again".

definition: Correct and exact, with no mistakes.
examples: The report must be accurate before we send it to the client.
His weather forecast was accurate all week.

pattern.example: Is this information accurate?

cloze.sentence: Please check that the figures in the invoice are ___.

formDrill.sentence: She described the accident ___ to the police.

fix.wrong: The news was not accuracy.
fix.right: The news was not accurate.
fix.why: Use the adjective "accurate" after "was".

distractors: Quick to be completed.
Very surprising to most people.
Based on opinion, not on facts.
tip: Accurate means correct; "precise" means exact in small detail. Something can be precise but not accurate.

definition: To feel true or meaningful to someone; also, to make a deep, echoing sound.
examples: Her story about starting over really resonated with the audience.
The sound of the drums resonated through the hall.

pattern.example: The speech resonated with young voters.

cloze.sentence: If an advert does not ___ with people, they will ignore it.

formDrill.sentence: The ___ of his words stayed with me for days.

fix.wrong: Her message resonated to me.
fix.right: Her message resonated with me.
fix.why: Use "resonate with" for the person who feels it.

distractors: To make someone feel confused.
To disagree strongly with someone.
To repeat words from memory.

definition: To make two different ideas agree, or to make people friends again after a fight.
examples: It is hard to reconcile a full-time job with studying.
The two brothers reconciled after years of silence.

pattern.rule: reconcile + A + with + B; reconcile with + person
pattern.example: She tried to reconcile her beliefs with her work.

cloze.sentence: The accountant had to ___ the bank statement with the company records.

formDrill.sentence: After the argument, there was a quick ___ between the friends.

fix.wrong: It is difficult to reconcile work to family.
fix.right: It is difficult to reconcile work with family.
fix.why: Use 'reconcile A with B'.

distractors: To divide something into equal parts.
To forget a past disagreement completely.
To compare two prices before buying.
tip: In accounting, to "reconcile" means to check that two sets of records match.
